program_overview.title: Ontario Grade 12 University Math: MHF4U and MCV4U
program_overview.tagline: A second teacher for Grade 12 university math: functions understood properly, then the calculus and vectors built on them, in step with your school course.
program_overview.description:
MHF4U and MCV4U are Ontario's Grade 12 university-preparation math courses. In the ministry's course list, MHF4U is titled Advanced Functions and MCV4U is titled Calculus and Vectors, both issued in 2007. The ministry lists the MHF4U prerequisite as "Functions, Grade 11, University Preparation, or Mathematics for College Technology, Grade 12, College Preparation", and it says "The new Advanced Functions course (MHF4U) must be taken prior to or concurrently with Calculus and Vectors (MCV4U)". Both courses also appear in university admission requirements. The University of Waterloo's Computer Science page asks for "Six Grade 12 U and/or M courses including" Advanced Functions and Calculus and Vectors, and the University of Toronto lists MCV4U as a prerequisite for computer science on all three campuses, with MHF4U also listed at Mississauga and Scarborough.

This course runs alongside the student's own MHF4U or MCV4U class, and many students take both in the same year. We follow the order of the student's school course outline, so what is learned here is used in class the same week. What our course teaches for MHF4U students: polynomial and rational functions, trigonometric functions in radians with identities and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions, combining functions, and rates of change. What it teaches for MCV4U students: limits and the derivative, the derivative rules, curve sketching and optimization, then vectors, lines and planes. Every topic starts from meaning, with graphs and small examples, before the algebra. Tests and assignments stay the student's own work: we explain, question and review, and the student does the math.

Please read this plainly: Modern Age Coders teaches alongside school and does not grant Ontario high school credits. Families who need the credit take the course through their school or a ministry-inspected credit provider. What we add is understanding, practice and confidence, in live classes with a real teacher.

phase_1_advanced_functions_part_1.title: PHASE 1: Advanced Functions, Part 1 (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_advanced_functions_part_1.description: The function toolkit every Grade 12 topic depends on, then polynomial and rational functions in depth.

month_1_function_toolkit_and_polynomials.title: Month 1: The Function Toolkit and Polynomial Functions

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Starting Point and the Function Toolkit
topics: A starting conversation and short diagnostic: the school, the course outline, the next test and the Grade 11 ideas to refresh
Function notation, domain and range, and reading a graph carefully
Transformations of functions: shifts, stretches and reflections
Inverse functions and what their graphs show
Factoring review: common factors, trinomials and the difference of squares
Setting up a clean notebook system for definitions, examples and mistakes
projects: A one-page function toolkit summary, with a sketch of each parent function and its transformations
week_1_2.practice: Short daily sets that mix new work with one or two Grade 11 refresher questions

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Polynomial Functions
topics: Degree, leading coefficient and end behaviour
Zeros, their order, and how the graph behaves at each zero
Sketching a polynomial from its factored form
Finding an equation from a graph or from given zeros
Even and odd functions and symmetry
Finite differences and what they say about degree
projects: A polynomial sketch set: ten polynomials sketched by hand from factored form, then checked with graphing technology
week_3_4.practice: For every sketch, write the end behaviour and the behaviour at each zero before drawing
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a short written test on functions and polynomial graphs, reviewed with written feedback

month_2_polynomial_equations_and_rationa.title: Month 2: Polynomial Equations and Rational Functions

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Polynomial Equations and Inequalities
topics: Polynomial long division and synthetic division
The remainder theorem and the factor theorem
Factoring cubics and quartics, including sums and differences of cubes
Solving polynomial equations exactly
Solving polynomial inequalities with a sign chart and a graph
Families of polynomials and word problems
projects: A worked solutions file for factoring and inequalities, with every step justified in words
week_5_6.practice: Mixed equation and inequality sets, with answers checked by substitution or graph

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Rational Functions
topics: Reciprocal functions and their graphs
Vertical and horizontal asymptotes, and holes
Sketching rational functions from their factored form
Solving rational equations and checking for restricted values
Solving rational inequalities with a sign chart
Average rate of change on a rational graph
projects: A rational function sketch set with asymptotes, intercepts and behaviour near each asymptote explained
week_7_8.practice: For every rational function, list restrictions and asymptotes first, then sketch
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a timed test on polynomial and rational functions in the style of a school unit test, marked with comments

phase_2_advanced_functions_part_2.title: PHASE 2: Advanced Functions, Part 2 (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_advanced_functions_part_2.description: Trigonometry in radians, exponential and logarithmic functions, combining functions and rates of change, with MHF4U exam review.

month_3_trigonometric_functions.title: Month 3: Trigonometric Functions, Identities and Equations

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Radians and Trigonometric Functions
topics: Radian measure and converting between radians and degrees
Special angles and the unit circle, without memorizing tables
Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent in radians
Amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical shift
Modelling periodic situations with sinusoidal functions
Reciprocal trigonometric functions and their graphs
projects: A sinusoidal model of a real periodic situation, with the equation built from the data and explained
week_9_10.practice: Unit circle and transformation sets, each answer checked against a quick sketch

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Identities and Trigonometric Equations
topics: Proving identities: working one side, and writing each step clearly
Compound angle formulas and double angle formulas
Solving linear and quadratic trigonometric equations in radians
Finding all solutions in a given interval
Equivalent trigonometric expressions using related angles
Common mistakes: dividing by a variable and losing solutions
projects: An identity proof file: ten identities proved in full, with the strategy for each written first
week_11_12.practice: One identity proof and two equations every day, with every solution in the interval listed
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a written test on trigonometric functions, identities and equations, reviewed with written feedback

month_4_exponential_logarithmic_and_comb.title: Month 4: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, Combining Functions and Rates of Change

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
topics: Exponential functions and their graphs, growth and decay
The logarithm as the inverse of an exponential function
Laws of logarithms and when each one applies
Solving exponential and logarithmic equations, and checking for extraneous roots
Changing the base of a logarithm
Applications: compound interest, half-life, sound and pH scales
projects: An applications pack: four real situations modelled with exponential or logarithmic functions and solved in full
week_13_14.practice: Mixed log law and equation sets, with each step named

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Combining Functions, Rates of Change and MHF4U Review
topics: Sums, differences, products and quotients of functions, and their graphs
Composition of functions and its domain
Average rate of change over an interval
Estimating instantaneous rate of change, the bridge to calculus
Choosing a function family to model a situation
MHF4U exam review: full solutions, communication and timed practice
projects: A personal MHF4U review pack: one-page summaries for each unit, a mistakes list and a reviewed timed paper
week_15_16.practice: Trace the meaning of a rate of change on a graph before calculating it
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a mixed MHF4U-style review paper, marked with written comments

phase_3_calculus_and_vectors.title: PHASE 3: Calculus and Vectors, and Exam Review (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_calculus_and_vectors.description: What we teach for MCV4U: limits and the derivative, derivative rules and applications, then vectors, lines and planes, ending with exam review. MCV4U batches begin with a quick review of the MHF4U ideas calculus relies on.

month_5_derivatives_and_applications.title: Month 5: Limits, Derivatives and Their Applications

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Rates of Change, Limits and the Derivative
topics: From average rate of change to instantaneous rate of change
Limits, explained with tables and graphs before algebra
The derivative from first principles
The power, constant multiple, sum and difference rules
The product, quotient and chain rules
The derivative as a slope and as a rate, in words and in units
projects: Three derivatives worked from first principles, then confirmed with the rules, with a short written explanation
week_17_18.practice: Daily derivative sets, each with one question asking what the derivative means in context

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Curve Sketching, Optimization and Rates
topics: Increasing and decreasing intervals, and local maxima and minima
Concavity and points of inflection from the second derivative
Sketching a curve from its derivatives
Optimization problems: setting up the function, the domain and the check
Derivatives of exponential and sinusoidal functions
Rates of change in motion: position, velocity and acceleration
projects: An optimization pack: four real problems set up and solved in full, each with a domain check
week_19_20.practice: For every optimization problem, write the function and its domain before differentiating
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a written test on derivatives and their applications, reviewed with written feedback

month_6_vectors_lines_planes_and_exam_re.title: Month 6: Vectors, Lines and Planes, and Exam Review

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Vectors in Two and Three Dimensions
topics: Geometric vectors: magnitude, direction, addition and scalar multiples
Cartesian vectors in two and three dimensions
The dot product, angles between vectors and projections
The cross product and what it measures
Applications: force, velocity and work
Drawing a clear diagram for every vector problem
projects: A vector applications set with a labelled diagram and a full written solution for each problem
week_21_22.practice: Short vector sets mixing geometric and Cartesian forms

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Lines and Planes, and Exam Review Technique
topics: Equations of lines in two and three dimensions: vector, parametric and symmetric forms
Equations of planes and their normal vectors
Intersections of lines and planes, and what each case looks like
Making a one-page summary for each unit of the school course
Full written solutions: showing reasoning so communication marks are earned
Timed review papers in the style of school exams, with careful review afterwards
projects: A personal MCV4U review pack: unit summaries, a mistakes list and two reviewed timed papers
week_23_24.practice: A timed mixed review each week, with every mistake written up and fixed
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: a timed review paper plus a short live walk-through of two of the student's own solutions

faqs.question: Does this course give my child an Ontario high school credit?
faqs.answer: No. Modern Age Coders teaches alongside school and does not grant Ontario high school credits. A family who needs the MHF4U or MCV4U credit takes the course through the student's school or a ministry-inspected credit provider. Our course helps the student understand and do well in the school course they are already taking.

faqs.question: What are MHF4U and MCV4U?
faqs.answer: They are Ontario's Grade 12 university-preparation math courses. In the ministry's course list, MHF4U is titled Advanced Functions and MCV4U is titled Calculus and Vectors. Your school's course outline gives the detail for your class. In our course, MHF4U students work on polynomial, rational, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions and rates of change, and MCV4U students work on derivatives and their applications, vectors, lines and planes.

faqs.question: What do I need before taking MHF4U?
faqs.answer: The ministry lists the MHF4U prerequisite as "Functions, Grade 11, University Preparation, or Mathematics for College Technology, Grade 12, College Preparation". Functions, Grade 11, University Preparation is MCR3U. In the first two weeks we refresh the Grade 11 ideas that Grade 12 relies on most.

faqs.question: Can my child take MHF4U and MCV4U at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many students do. The ministry says "The new Advanced Functions course (MHF4U) must be taken prior to or concurrently with Calculus and Vectors (MCV4U)". When a student takes both at once, we follow both school course outlines and review each MHF4U idea just before calculus needs it.

faqs.question: Is MCV4U hard?
faqs.answer: It asks for more independence than earlier math courses, and it builds on everything in MHF4U, so a gap in functions shows up quickly in calculus. That is why we teach meaning before algebra, keep a mistakes list, and practise a little every day. Most of the difficulty eases once a student understands what a derivative means rather than only how to compute one.

faqs.question: Do universities ask for MHF4U and MCV4U for computer science?
faqs.answer: Many do. The University of Waterloo's Computer Science page asks for "Six Grade 12 U and/or M courses including" Advanced Functions, Calculus and Vectors, "Any Grade 12 U English" and "One other 4U course". At the University of Toronto, St. George lists "MCV4U" as a computer science prerequisite, while Mississauga and Scarborough list both "MHF4U" and "MCV4U". Always check each university's current admission page. We make no admission promises; we help the student build real understanding.

faqs.question: Does the course follow my school's order?
faqs.answer: Yes. Schools order the units differently, so we use the student's own course outline and next test date to set the pace. The plan on this page shows our standard sequence, and each batch follows the order of its students' schools as closely as possible.

faqs.question: Will you do my child's assignments or tests?
faqs.answer: No. School work stays the student's own. We explain concepts, ask questions, review work the student has written and suggest how to improve it, and we follow the school's rules on outside help. That is also the only kind of help that lasts into the exam room.

faqs.question: Can you help with exam review?
faqs.answer: Yes. The course teaches exam technique directly: one-page unit summaries, full written solutions that show reasoning, and timed review papers with careful review afterwards. We also use the teacher's exam outline so revision matches what will actually be assessed.

faqs.question: Can my child join partway through the school year?
faqs.answer: Yes, the course is joinable any month. We start from the student's current unit and next test, fill gaps from earlier units as needed, and keep pace with the school course from then on.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or 1-on-1. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher looks at where your child is in MHF4U or MCV4U, works through a short problem with them, and suggests whether group, mini batch or 1-on-1 classes fit best. There is no obligation to enrol.
